newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's ruling party confident as polls close.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's ruling party confident as polls close.

text.p: Singapore ended voting in general elections on Thursday with the focus on whether the opposition could hold, or even improve on, its paltry number of seats in parliament.
The People's Action Party (PAP), never out of power since independence in 1965, was already assured of a majority in the 83-member parliament because the opposition contested only 36 seats.
But Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong has staked his prestige on keeping the opposition to a minimum in parliament and top colleagues said the PAP was confident of doing so.
"We're quite confident," Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong told state television.
Goh told state radio the government had been successful in controlling the agenda throughout the campaign.
He said the government was happy with its election strategy against the opposition, which held only four seats in the outgoing parliament.

Voting is compulsory in Singapore and most of the 760,000 voters out of the city-state's three million people cast their votes in polling centres which closed at 8 pm local time (1200 GMT). Long lines of voters had begun forming early in the morning.
The campaign featured tough words, threats of lawsuits and a row between the PAP and the United States.

As counting began, all eyes were on the constituency of Cheng San, where a bitter war of words broke out in the campaign between Goh and Worker's Party (WP) candidate Tang Liang Hong over claims of racial chauvinism.

In the heat of the campaign on Wednesday, Tang filed two complaints to police against Goh and several ministers, alleging that PAP leaders defamed him by making statements leading the public to believe Tang was an anti-Christian Chinese chauvinist, a stance which would be anathema in Singapore's multi-racial society, which still remembers race riots in the 1960s.
Goh said he would sue Tang, accusing the WP candidate of calling him a liar.

State television said Tang asked for police protection but Goh, who was returned unopposed in his own seat, told reporters there was no need for it, saying the campaigns were orderly and people had not been incited to violence.
Cheng San is a multi-member constituency which elects five MPs in a winner-takes-all contest. A win for the opposition Workers' Party (WP) would be an unprecedented victory.
The four seats the opposition won in 1991 was its best showing. Political analysts say defeat for the PAP in Cheng San could damage Goh's reputation as a strong leader capable of winning elections.
"If the opposition wins eight to 10 seats, it could jeopardise Goh's premiership," said Bruce Gale, an analyst at Political and Economic Risk Consultancy.
The PAP has ruled Singapore since 1959, transforming it through strict control into a prosperous city where average per capita income is higher than in Britain, the old colonial power.
But opposition parties have campaigned hard on the issue of having an alternative voice in parliament and a check on the PAP's dominance.
The key campaign issue for the ruling party has been its promise of a multi-billion dollar programme to upgrade public housing to lure voters away from the opposition.
Goh told voters that areas which return opposition MPs would miss out in the programme and risk becoming slums in 20 to 30 years.
That campaign strategy drew criticism from the U.S. State Department and a furious retort from Goh, who accused Washington of interfering.
